issues.legal_issue: Excluding pre-arrest bail for offences arising from the practice of untouchability does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality.
material_facts: The challenged provision excluded pre-arrest bail in cases involving accusations of offences against members of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
The offences at issue were connected to the practice of untouchability and formed a distinct category from ordinary offences.

The legislative background described members of these communities as vulnerable to intimidation when they asserted their rights, and the Court considered that accused persons released on pre-arrest bail could intimidate victims or obstruct prosecution.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion of pre-arrest bail for the covered offences does not violate the constitutional guarantee of equality because those offences form a distinct class and can be treated differently from other offences.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the offences as a distinct class because they arise from the practice of untouchability and the social conditions that give rise to them differ from those associated with ordinary offences. It relied on Article 17 of the Constitution, the purpose and legislative background of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and Jai Singh v. Union of India, AIR 1993 Rajasthan 117.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_prearrest_ba: A person challenges the exclusion of pre-arrest bail for a defined category of offences on equality grounds.
predicates.covered_offences_arise_from_untouchabili: The offences covered by the exclusion arise from the practice of untouchability.
predicates.victims_are_vulnerable_to_intimidation: Members of the targeted community are vulnerable to intimidation that may deter them from pursuing complaints or prosecution.
predicates.covered_offences_are_distinct_from_ordin: The covered offences and the social conditions giving rise to them form a distinct class from ordinary offences.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a pre-arrest-bail exclusion on equality grounds, and the covered offences arise from untouchability, their victims are vulnerable to intimidation, and the offences form a distinct class, the exclusion does not violate equality.

issues.legal_issue: Excluding pre-arrest bail for a special category of offences does not violate the constitutional protection of life and personal liberty because pre-arrest bail is not an essential ingredient of that protection.
material_facts: The challenged provision made pre-arrest bail unavailable in cases involving accusations of offences under the special legislation.
Pre-arrest bail was first introduced by the 1973 Code of Criminal Procedure; it did not exist in the earlier Code.
The power to grant pre-arrest bail was conferred on the High Court and Court of Session and was discretionary rather than an automatic right.
The Court considered the risk that accused persons released on pre-arrest bail could intimidate victims or obstruct proper investigation.
issues.conclusion: The exclusion of pre-arrest bail for the covered offences does not violate the constitutional protection of life and personal liberty.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that pre-arrest bail is a statutory right introduced after the Constitution came into force, is discretionary, and is not an essential ingredient of the right to life and personal liberty. It relied on Article 21 of the Constitution, the 41st Report of the Law Commission, and Kartar Singh v. State of Punjab, JT 1994 (2) SC 423, which upheld a comparable exclusion of pre-arrest bail.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_prearrest_ba: A person challenges the exclusion of pre-arrest bail for a defined category of offences on personal-liberty grounds.
predicates.prearrest_bail_is_a_later_statutory_disc: Pre-arrest bail was created by legislation after the Constitution came into force and is granted through a court's discretion rather than as an automatic entitlement.
predicates.covered_offences_carry_risk_of_victim_in: The circumstances surrounding the covered offences create a risk that an accused person at liberty before arrest could intimidate victims or obstruct investigation.

issues.definition: When a person challenges a pre-arrest-bail exclusion on personal-liberty grounds, pre-arrest bail is a later statutory discretion, and the covered offences create a risk of victim intimidation or investigative obstruction, the exclusion does not violate personal liberty.
